story_pergunta: At your company, who decides what an AI agent is allowed to do?

slides.eyebrow: AI ON THE RISE · UNITED AIRLINES
slides.headline: United bans AI agents from booking flights for travelers
slides.sub: The agent was not the problem. The missing rules were.

slides.headline: United is blocking outside AI agents from making reservations
slides.body: United says sharing credentials with third-party AI assistants can expose sensitive information and cause unintended purchases. It is restricting access on its own platforms and through agencies and aggregators. Southwest took the opposite tack and opened its inventory to ChatGPT users.

slides.headline: What this signals about agents that buy for customers
items: The business decides whether an outside agent may act at all
Credentials and payments are where the risk concentrates
Two airlines, two opposite policies on the same technology

slides.headline: What I see in companies: the agent ships before the rules exist
items: Nobody defines where the agent may act and where it may not
Access to payments and data is granted before anyone decides who is liable
The company does not control the channel, so it cannot control the outcome

slides.headline: A building materials store in southern Brazil: an agent inside its own channel
items: AI sales rep on WhatsApp: one agent and three tools, 9 nodes in the whole flow
Rules: no made-up specs, never reveals stock, never gives discounts
65 out of 65 real customer questions found the right product

slides.headline: Simple that works beats complex that impresses.
slides.body: United is drawing a line around where an agent may act. In practice, that is the right question to start with. An agent with a defined channel, a few tools and hard rules is easier to trust and easier to measure than one with open access.

slides.eyebrow: WANT TO SEE HOW I DID IT?
slides.headline: Comment SDR.
slides.body: I'll send you the step-by-step of this case by DM. I take AI off the drawing board and put it into production, with measured results.

caption:
United Airlines said it is banning third-party AI agents from booking flights on travelers' behalf. Its reasons: security risks around shared credentials, unintended purchases, and possible conflicts with federal rules. Southwest went the other way and opened its inventory to ChatGPT users.

What I see in companies is the same gap on a smaller scale. The agent gets built, but nobody defines where it may act, what it can touch and what it must never do. Then it either stalls or creates risk.

I built an AI sales rep on WhatsApp for a building materials store in southern Brazil. It works inside a channel the business controls. One agent, three tools (search, size a heater, call a human salesperson), 9 nodes in the whole flow. Rules are fixed: no made-up specs, never reveals stock, never gives discounts. Result: 65 out of 65 real customer questions found the right product.

Agents that act for customers scale when the business defines the channel and the rules first. Design those before you ship the agent.

Comment SDR and I'll DM you how I did it.

Sources: cbsnews.com
